notes.short: Gideon would not rule; Abimelech sought the crown
notes.about: The leaders of Shechem make Abimelech king. His father Gideon had turned that rule down: “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.” The son, with no call from God, takes for himself the rule his father refused, and gains it by murdering his brothers.

sides.label: Seeks the crown, and takes it
sides.words: proceeded to make Abimelech their king

sides.label: Refuses to rule
sides.words: I will not rule over you, nor will my son.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: Abimelech set out to take his father's place directly against his father's will, since Gideon had said no son of his should rule, and he had no call from God as his father had, only his own ambition. F. W. Farrar (Ellicott's Commentary), on the crowning: Abimelech was the first Israelite to bear the name of king, while Gideon had refused the title of king and even of ruler.
notes.limit: The contrast is in how each stood toward the crown, not in the whole of Gideon's life: his gold ephod “became a snare to Gideon and his household.”

cites.quote: nothing will serve his proud spirit but he will succeed him in the government of Israel, directly contrary to his father's will, for he had declared no son of his should rule over them. He had no call from God to this honour as his father had
He was the first Israelite who ever bore that name. ... Gideon had not only refused the title of king (melek), but even the title of ruler (Jdg 8:23).
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “Let them save you”: the LORD's irony
notes.about: When Israel cries out, the LORD tells them to cry to the gods they have chosen and let those gods save them. Those gods could neither hear nor save, so the words expose the folly of serving them. Israel then put away the foreign gods (verse 16).

figure.name: Irony
figure.means: that the gods they had chosen could neither hear them nor save them

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under irony spoken by God: those gods could neither hear nor deliver. Henry says the LORD lets Israel see their folly in serving gods that could not help them when they most needed help, bidding them try what those gods can do for them now, to stir them to true repentance.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Divine Irony, p. 808
cites.quote: This was Divine Sarcasm, for those gods could neither hear nor deliver.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: To awaken them to a thorough repentance and reformation, he lets them see, (1.) Their folly in serving Baalim. They had been at a vast expense to obtain the favour of such gods as could not help them when they had most need of their help: "Go, and cry unto the gods which you have chosen ... try what they can do for you now.

notes.short: “Relieving himself” renders a modest Hebrew phrase
notes.about: Finding the doors locked, Eglon's servants suppose their king is relieving himself. The Hebrew says this modestly: literally, he is covering his feet, probably because a man's long garments fell over his feet as he stooped. The same phrase is used of Saul in the cave (1 Samuel 24:3).

figure.name: Euphemism
figure.means: easing nature, said modestly; the Hebrew is literally covering his feet

original.note: In Hebrew the phrase is literally covering (sakak) his feet (regel).

notes.evidence: Bullinger says covering the feet is put for a duty of nature, because the garments fell over the feet as a man stooped, and calls it Euphemy. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the phrase a euphemism for the necessities of nature, and F. W. Farrar (Ellicott) calls it an Eastern euphemism. Keil points to 1 Samuel 24:3.
notes.limit: Some read the Hebrew phrase instead as lying down to sleep with the feet covered, which would also explain why the servants waited so long (verse 25).

cites.quote: To cover the feet is put for performing a duty of nature, because when stooping the garments fell over the feet. This is a beautiful example of Euphemy
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: they thought "surely (אך, lit. only, nothing but) he covers his feet" (a euphemism for performing the necessities of nature; cf. Sa1 24:3 )
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is an Eastern euphemism taken from spreading out the garments while relieving the needs of nature
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.about: Sisera's fall is told in short clauses with no “and” between them: he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still. The words do not stop over each movement but hurry on to the end of the verse, where he fell dead.

figure.name: Asyndeton
figure.words: At her feet he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still; at her feet he collapsed, he fell; where he collapsed, there he fell dead.
figure.means: the movements of his fall, set down with no “and”, hurrying on to the last words: he fell dead

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Judges 5:27 among his examples of Asyndeton (no-ands), the figure in which the reader is hurried over the separate statements to the climax they lead up to.
notes.limit: The note claims only the missing “and”; the phrase repeated at the start of the clauses is a separate figure.

cites.quote: When the figure Asyndeton is used, we are not detained over the separate statements ... but we are hurried on over the various matters that are mentioned, as though they were of no account, in comparison with the great climax to which they lead up ... At her feet he bowed ... where he bowed, there he fell down dead.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.about: The angel of the LORD recalls what Israel was forbidden, a covenant with the people of the land, and what they were commanded, to tear down their altars. The charge comes back in reverse: the command was not obeyed, and the forbidden thing was done.

lines.words: and you are not to make a covenant with the people of this land,
but you shall tear down their altars.
Yet you have not obeyed My voice.
What is this you have done?

notes.evidence: Boys sets the verse out in four lines: a thing forbidden in the first and a thing commanded in the second; the guilt for each appears in turn, the commanded thing left undone in the third and the forbidden thing done in the fourth.

cites.quote: In a. we have a thing forbidden … in b. a thing commanded … The guilt of the Israelites, in each particular, appears, in b. and a. They had done that which was forbidden … They had left undone that which was commanded … Thus a. answers to a., and b. to b.
cites.read: the 1825 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/akeytobookpsalm00boysgoog

notes.short: Sisera's mother's hopeful words end in silence
notes.about: Sisera's mother waits at her window and keeps telling herself that dividing the spoil explains his delay. Her words stop there. The song does not tell of her disappointment or how she bears it; it breaks out instead, “So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD!”

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.words: for the neck of the looter
figure.means: her hopeful words end there; her disappointment, and how she bears it, are left untold

notes.evidence: Bullinger calls this a wonderful Aposiopesis: her soliloquy ends in a sudden silence, and how she bears it is left to the imagination. Farrar (Ellicott's Commentary) finds the song's abrupt rush to its close very grand: by leaving the princesses' disappointment unspoken, in scorn, it implies it all the more forcibly.

cites.quote: There is a wonderful Aposiopesis here, where the mother of Sisera looks out of her lattice and wonders where Sisera is, and why he does not return. ... Her soliloquy ends in a sudden silence. Everything is left to the imagination as to how she bears it.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The abrupt burst in which the song rushes, as it were, to its conclusion, is very grand. The total frustration of the hopes of the princesses is all the more forcibly implied by the scorn with which it is left unexpressed.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Jotham's trees picture the crowning of Abimelech
notes.about: Jotham tells of trees looking for a king. The olive tree, the fig tree and the grapevine will not leave their fruit to rule; only the thornbush accepts. From verse 16 Jotham applies the story to the leaders of Shechem, who had made Abimelech king.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the trees set out to anoint a king for themselves
figure.means: the leaders of Shechem choosing a king; the worthless thornbush that takes the crown is Abimelech

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Judges 9:7-15 under Allegory as a continued Hypocatastasis: only the trees are named, and the interpretation in verses 16-20 makes the meaning plain. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) takes the fruitful trees as nobler men in general and the briar as a worthless man; Henry sees Abimelech in the bramble; Hervey (Barnes' Notes) says Gideon's house refused the kingdom and Abimelech took it.
notes.limit: Some of these writers call the story a fable or a parable. They differ on the three fruitful trees: two see Gideon and others who had turned the kingship down, one sees worthy and fruitful men in general.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 749
cites.quote: It is a continued Hypocatastasis, only one of the two things being plainly mentioned. Were it not for the interpretation given, in verses 16-20, there would be nothing beyond what is implied.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The meaning of the fable is very easy to understand. The olive tree, fig tree, and vine do not represent different historical persons ... but in a perfectly general way the nobler families or persons who bring forth fruit and blessing in the calling appointed them by God ... The briar, which has nothing but thorns upon it ... is an admirable simile for a worthless man
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: His parable is very ingenious ... He hereby applauds the generous modesty of Gideon, and the other judges who were before him, and perhaps of the sons of Gideon, who had declined accepting the state and power of kings when they might have had them ... He hereby exposes the ridiculous ambition of Abimelech, whom he compares to the bramble or thistle

The application is obvious. The noble Gideon and his worthy sons had declined the proffered kingdom. The vile, base-born Abimelech had accepted it, and his act would turn out to the mutual ruin of himself and his subjects.

notes.short: Samson's riddle of the lion and the honey
notes.about: Samson's riddle is drawn from the lion he killed and the honey he later found in its body (14:8). The eater and the strong one is the lion; the food and the sweet thing is the honey. The men gave the answer (14:18) only after his wife told it to them (14:17).

figure.name: Riddle
figure.words: Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet.
figure.means: the lion Samson had killed, in whose carcass he later found bees and honey

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Samson's saying under Ænigma, a dark saying, and points to the answer in verse 18. Henry explains that food came from the devourer, and that the men had only to think of the strongest eater and the sweetest food. Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the riddle was about honey in the lion's carcass.
notes.limit: Some writers also draw lessons from the riddle, about God bringing good out of evil or about Christ; the note keeps to the lion and the honey that the text itself gives.

cites.quote: The answer is given in verse 18, in the form of another question ... “What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?” This is a saying both “dark” and “deep”: for there is precious truth hidden in that darkness and those depths, which neither the Philistines nor the natural man can understand or receive. The Living Word (Christ) is stronger than the strong man armed
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: yet food came from the devourer ... If they had but so much sense as to consider what eater is most strong, and what meat is most sweet, they would have found out the riddle, and neither lions nor honey were such strangers to their country ... This riddle is applicable to many of the methods of divine providence and grace. When God, by an over-ruling providence, brings good out of evil
Samson's riddle related to honey in the lion's carcass. ... Three days were passed in vain attempts to unravel the enigma.
